courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Experiencing Architecture
courses.description:
(UGEC1016 is double-coded with ARCH1320.)

The course provides a general outline to architecture. The aim is to introduce architecture as a cultural phenomenon. The course will increase the student's awareness of the built environment as it exists all around. It examines a variety of spatial experiences encountered in exemplary places and buildings. The scope of the course is not limited to buildings alone, but includes cities and landscapes as extensions of architecture. The course introduces a range of topics, including the historical, symbolic, aesthetic, functional, cultural and green aspects of architecture.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC1016 is double-coded with ARCH1320. 
Not for Architectural Studies Majors; and students who have taken ARCH1320[1330] or 2111.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
To comprehend the discipline of architecture in relation to the broader contexts of history, culture and civilization.

To remember the key concepts and some significant works of architecture.

To analyze the relationship between architecture, city, and landscape, cultural memory.

To comprehend the design and building process of architecture.

To enrich students with direct dialogue with the architects/designers who have created the architecture.

To apply skills for clear expression in written and oral presentations.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course introduces a number of topics related to the conceptual and aesthetic aspects of architecture. Among the topics introduced will be the following:

* Introduction of Architectural Vocabulary

* A Brief History of Hong Kong Architecture

* Architecture through the Ages

* Architecture and Culture

* Architecture and Heritage

* Green Architecture

* The Design Process

* The Building Process and Architectural Practice

* China New Architecture

The course format involves regular lecture sessions, with occasional discussion sessions and short group presentations. The course may also include occasional field trips/excursions to selected sites in Hong Kong as well as some workshop exercises.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Globalization of Korean Popular Culture
courses.description: This course is designed to introduce students to contemporary Korean popular culture, and more specifically the 21st century South Korean cultural phenomenon called Hallyu (Korean wave) – its promises and limitations as well as its popularity and backlash against it. By taking an interdisciplinary approach to the topic, we will study food, film, television, music, fashion and sports and ask how they participate in the transnational production, distribution and circulation of culture, identity, modernity, tradition, ideology and politics both regionally and globally. One of the major questions this course will explore is the curious ways in which these popular media continuously re-stage and re-define Korea’s historical past in order to comment on its present. This course also targets to equip students with analytical tools to critically think about popular culture as well as understand theories of cultural globalization.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Global Studies (GLBS and GLSD) Majors; and students who have taken GLBS3202 or 3402.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To identify the historical developments and current content trends of the Korean wave.

2. To analyze the causes and outcomes of the Korean wave.

3. To recognize the importance of critical thinking skills for analyzing the transnational media content and effects in a global, cultural context.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Politics, Law and Society
courses.description:
(UGEC1814 is double-coded with GPAD1100.)

This course aims to provide an introductory examination of legal systems and the role of law in the shifting social and political contexts. Interdisciplinary perspectives (e.g. philosophical, political and sociological etc.) will be taken on to deal with the conceptual and empirical issues. The course is not designed for professional legal training, but aims to assist students to reflect on the legal phenomena they experience in their daily life.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC1814 is double-coded with GPAD1100. 
Not for Government and Public Administration Majors; and students who have taken GPAD1100.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
* *On knowledge and comprehension level**

Students are expected to recognize and have basic understanding on a broad conceptual vocabulary and analytical approaches in legal discussion.

* *On application level**

Students are expected to command writing skills to convey legal and political concepts and analysis.

Students are expected to command presentation skills to convey legal political concepts and analysis.

Students are expected to identify and recognize legal issues in the shifting social and political contexts, through the lens of the legal conceptual vocabularies and analytical approaches.

* *On analysis level**

Students are expected to be able to analyze different perspectives, values and theories in relation to the controversial legal issues.

* *On synthesis level**

From the interdisciplinary perspectives and intellectual horizons the course provides, students are expected to develop critical analytical skills, so that their self-expression and communication with other people will be improved.

* *On evaluation level**

Students are expected to formulate one’s own view in understanding the legal issues, and the basic jurisprudential debates about the nature of law behind them

* *Conceptual issues**

Topic 1: Introduction: Politics, Law and Society

Topic 2: Natural Law vs. Legal Positivism

Topic 3: The Ideal of Public Law: Constitutional Government and the Rule of Law

Topic 4: Constitutionalism and Judicial Review

Topic 5: The Obligation to Obey the Law vs. Civil Disobedience

* *Law in action**

Topic 6: Legal System and Process

Topic 8: Law and Social Order: Formal and Informal Systems of Criminal Justice

* *Law in Chinese context**

Topic 9: Chinese Legal Tradition and Its Modernization

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Sociology and Modern Society
courses.description:
(UGEC1823 is double-coded with SOCI1102.)

This course explores into the significance of sociological perspectives in understanding modern society. Attention will be given to the application of sociological concepts in the observation and analysis of social phenomena in modern society. The course is designed particularly to develop intellectual skills, as part of a student's general education, for a better understanding of the nature of modern society.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC1823 is double-coded with SOCI1102.
Not for Sociology Majors; and students who have taken SOCI1001 or 1102.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
- Students will gain exposure to a diverse set of sociological research, and understand how the relevant concepts and theories can be applied to modern societies.

- Students will develop an understanding of the constitutive relations between the economic, political, social, and cultural domains in society, thereby gaining a new perspective on their own lives and the world around them.

- Students will learn to develop their own analytical framework through active participation in discussion and completion of essay type test questions. These will enhance their general knowledge and skills in critical thinking.
courses.course_syllabus:
CORE CONTENT

1. Sociology as a social science discipline

- What is a social science explanation?

- Variety of sociological explanations

2. Rise of modernity

- With special reference to the insights of Durkheim, Weber, and Marx.

3. The Internet society and globalization

- Nature of postindustrial society and information society

- Virtual community v. traditional community

- The small world phenomenon: Insights from social network research

4. Consumer society

- Nature of advanced capitalism

- Economic sociology of market demand

5. Marriage and family

- The changing conceptions of marriage and consequences of the changes

- Theoretical debates among such theories as sociobiology, social conflict, rational choice

6. Socioeconomic inequality and status competition in modern society

- The root sources of inequality: classic and contemporary theories

- Rising inequality in the USA and East Asia

- Status competition

7. Selected topics

- For examples: Theories and evidence on modern schooling, gender and work, deviance and social control, social movement, democratization, health and health care, third world development.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Wine Culture and Appreciation: Enhancing Quality of Life
courses.description:
Wine weaves in with human history from its very beginnings and has developed into one of the foremost products of civilization. Wine has its roots in the customs, traditions and history and it occupies an important place in the culture and life of the people worldwide.

The purpose of this course is to lead students on a cultural journey around the world and introduce them to a historical perspective on wine and its place in society. It is a course addressing the science of wine, the world wine regions, and the role of wine in human culture. Specifically, the course is designed to increase students’ understanding of essential wine knowledge and culture and help them build a strong base for lifelong wine appreciation and enhance their quality of life. The topics include cultural history of wine, the identification of grape varieties, the methods of viticulture (grape cultivation) and the techniques of vinification (wine making). The impact of alcoholic beverages on society and human physiology will be emphasized. Comparative tasting methods will be introduced through sensory evaluations training.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for Hotel and Tourism Management (HTMGN); Hospitality and Real Estate (HTMGB) Majors; and students who have taken GEUC2017.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will have attained the knowledge necessary to appreciate, select, and taste wines with confidence. In particular, the students should be able to:

1. Address the role of wine in society, history and civilization
2. Examine the impact of alcohol consumption on health and social issues raised by alcohol abuse
3. Discuss tradition, diversity and geographical characteristics of wines and different systems of denoting wine quality in the social, historical and cultural context.
4. Develop senses of sight, smell and taste in appreciating different types of wines for sensory attributes, varietal character, and terroir
5. Recognize the impact of globalization on wine trade and the economy, using Hong Kong as the regional wine hub as an example.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course will address the following perspectives:

* *1. Wine, culture and society**

* Wine and civilization
* Wine and cuisine
* Wine and music and arts
* The poets’ homage

* *2. A Survey of wine history**

* Origin and development of wine and role of wine in society
* Wine in Western versus Eastern Culture

* *3. Globalization and wine**

* The impact of globalization on wine industry regarding history, culture, geography, major wine regions
* Wine labeling law, economic impact of wine production

* *4. Hong Kong as the regional wine hub**

* Economic and social impact
* Wine culture in Hong Kong

* *5. Vine and Wine**

* Grape cultivation - viticulture

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Modernity and Urban Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2042 is double-coded with CURE2016.)

This course is an introduction to the formation of modernity in relation to various aspects of urban culture. Tracing the development of cities and the urban cultures evolved within the new urban development since the 19th Century, cities such as Paris, London, New York will serve as 'texts' for analysis. Architecture, urban planning, artistic and intellectual movements as well as modes of everyday life in urban living are studied to demonstrate how the modern ways of thinking, seeing and living come into being. The course will also focus on the specificity of Hong Kong's experience in urban development and its adaptation of 'modernity' during a process of urbanization. The course will employ a wide range of visual images and audio-visual materials to explain the dynamism between modernity and urban culture.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Food and Hunger
courses.description: Food is essential for life by providing energy and nutrition and achieving zero hunger is one of 17 Sustainable Development Goals in the United Nations’ 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The course adopts a multidisciplinary approach to examine the different issues of food and hunger, and how they change over time. The causes of world hunger will be analyzed with special emphasis on food production systems, bearing in mind there is no single solution to the problem. Moreover, the course delves into the economic, social, and environmental dimensions of hunger, examining how issues such as poverty, food insecurity, and climate change intersect to exacerbate the problem. Towards the end of the course, students will gain a deeper understanding of Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger) through an exploration of sustainable agricultural practices and strategies to address global hunger challenges in the 21st century. Lectures will be supplemented with case studies, videos and slides.

courses.title: Discovering Africa: Environment, Society and Prospects
courses.description:
Popular representations of the African continent produced in global discussions are marked by a stereotyped image of Africa, its culture, environment and development. The purpose of this course is to critically examine the common framing of Africa as a continent of conflict, disasters, poverty and a region that is perpetually in need of external intervention. In addition to the myth that surrounds Africa, there is a growing dynamics of activities resulting into the current interest on the continent.

Earlier, the UN settled on the Agenda 2030 as a plan of action for people, planet and prosperity for the whole world. This plan dovetails very well with the Africa’s Agenda 2063. This therefore provides an opportunity to identify where Africa situates on SDG issues that include its people, its environment and its economic development.

The course will therefore present to students the context of Africa relating to its geography, environment, culture as well as contemporary development issues shaping the destiny of Africa. Through lectures, guest speakers, videos and possibly field studies, students will be able to critically evaluate the stereotypical notion of Africa as a continent rather than as a country as is quite often misconstrued. The course will provide an intellectual platform to understand and analyze issues from a multi-disciplinary perspective as they relate to Africa and humanity. The students will be able to interpret and explain in broad terms, the contemporary position of Africa as it relates to other parts of the world with special attention to its relationship with Asia and China in particular.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Living in the Anthropocene: Nature, Culture and Power
courses.description:
(UGEC2243 is double-coded with CURE2018.)

Human have altered the environment in ways that have no precedence in human history. Ecological crisis, environmental degradation, and extreme weathers have become the watchwords of contemporary politics. The conventional boundaries between “nature” and “culture” are now being questioned. How do nature, culture and power intersect in our everyday life? How do we get to understand issues of sustainability and environmental crisis from a broad historical perspective and global activism angle? How are gender, class and race interact with technology, damaged environment, animal and plant species? This course explores these questions and the rich debates in the emerging field of environmental humanity and literature of the Anthropocene.

Class topics are organized on major global green movements that resisted oil pollution, toxic factories, logging companies, dam constructions and nuclear plant building. Students get to learn the historical developments of major environmental activism in the West and the global south. How was the Greenpeace founded? What is the Narmada Dam Movement in India? Do you know Ken Saro-Wiwa, an environmental activist against Shell oil pollution in Nigeria? In each class we examine historical texts, visual materials and theoretical debates to explore how environmental justice has been intertwined with histories of colonialism, neoliberalism, and questions of gender, race, poverty and class. Together the class explores the problem of the Anthropocene (Nature) in the context of colonial history, grass root struggles (Culture) and corporation greed (Power).

This course addresses many of the 17 United Nation Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Climate Actions (13), Life on Land (15), Life below Water (14), Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions (16), Clean Energy (7), Reduced Inequalities (10), and Gender Inequality (5). Students are able to identify the weekly course content aligned with specific SDGs and be able to understand these goals in both historical and contemporary contexts.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Celebrity, Stardom, and Hong Kong Popular Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2245 is double-coded with CURE2007.)
Celebrity culture is generally understood as a cult full of short-lived trends and inconsequential fan behaviour. We seldom consider, however, the powerful influence it has over our cultural identities. This course examines how the interplay between celebrity culture and the cultural industry shapes cultural identity with case studies from Hong Kong as the major scope of study. Starting with a brief history of Hong Kong celebrity culture from the 1980s to the present day, the course offers an entry point for students to understand the intricate relationship between the media and celebrity culture, encompassing a wide range of cultural icons and phenomena such as action film actors, cross-media megastars, and YouTube micro-celebrities. Each case study will engage with key concepts in celebrity culture, such as star-text, commodification, authenticity, extratextual reading, and participatory reading. The course proceeds by introducing the critical perspective of cultural studies in making sense of representation politics, public culture, fandom studies, and the diverse modes of intimacy in the digital age. Overall, students will gain an understanding of celebrity culture and how identities are thus produced, promoted, and commodified in the wider arena of media and popular culture.

courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of the subject, students will be able to:

* **Define and explain** the connotation of celebrity culture, stardom, and popular culture in contemporary society, and the genealogy of discourses development of Hong Kong popular culture over time.
* **Understand** on how cultural identities are shaped by the interplay between celebrity culture and the popular culture industry.
* **Employ** a selected range of methods to study the development and formation of celebrity culture and infer the meaning of such process in the Hong Kong context.
* **Reflect** on the impact of celebrity culture on the formation of cultural identities.
* **Demonstrate** the intersectionality of celebrity culture and the formation of cultural identities locally and globally.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Class 1 Introduction: Why Does Celebrity Culture Matter?**

* Introducing the basics of celebrity culture and the importance of studying celebrity and stardom
* Outlining the development timeline of Hong Kong celebrity culture from the 1980s to the 2020s

* *Class 2 Star Image and Star Text: Bruce Lee**

* Analysing the production and consumption of film stars and their star image
* Synthesizing the critical concepts of ‘star-text’ in celebrity studies and ‘textual analysis’ in cultural studies
* Assessing Bruce Lee as a star text in relation to the concept of ‘representation’
* Integrating the case of Bruce Lee with the identity formation of Hong Kongers as modern citizens

* *Class 3 The Social Phenomenon of Stars: Leslie Cheung**

* Discussing the critical concept of ‘extratextual reading’ in celebrity studies
* Assessing Leslie Cheung as a star text in relation to the concept of queer stardom and posthumous fame.
* Integrating the case of Leslie Cheung with the identity formation of Hong Kongers as cosmopolitan

* *Class 4 Discussion Panel (I)**

* Students will work in groups to create a presentation about their favourite Hong Kong film star. Presentations should be submitted online via Blackboard.
* Each group will then be assigned to review another group’s presentation. They will analyze the assigned work and apply one concept from Class 1-3 in their critique.

* *Class 5 Cross-media Megastar (1): Anita Mui**

* Interpreting the concept of ‘commodification’ in cultural studies in relation to Anita Mui's on-screen persona.
* Demonstrating the influence of popular music on stardom and celebrity culture

* *Class 6 Cross-media Megastar (2): Twins**

* Theorizing ‘celebrity-commodity’ in celebrity studies and mapping the culture industry in the 2000s
* Examining how the industry of popular culture in Hong Kong gives rise to cross-media megastars
* Evaluating ways in which the stardom of the cross-media megastar influences the formation of Hong Kong cultural identity

* *Class 7 On the Politics of Authenticity: ‘Real’ Celebrity and Reality Shows**

* Discussing the concept of ‘authenticity’ in celebrity studies and media studies.
* Critiquing how television channels have produced stars and singers via talent shows and reality shows from 2000s to 2010s
* Comparing two local TV shows, Minutes to Fame (殘酷一叮) and Good Night Show – King Maker (全民造星) in their creation of ‘ordinary celebrities’

* *Class 8 Discussion Panel (II)**

* Students will work in groups to create a presentation about their favourite Hong Kong singer. Presentations should be submitted online via Blackboard.
* Each group will then be assigned to review another group’s presentation. They will analyze the assigned work and apply one concept from Class 5-7 in their critique.

* *Class 9 Stars, Consumption, and Public Culture (1): Anthony Wong, Anson Lo, and Jeremy Lee**

* Discussing the concepts of ‘celebrity consumption’ and ‘participatory reading’
* Examining the ‘campness’ of the star image of Anthony Wong, Anson Lo, and Jeremy Lee
* Integrating the practice of ‘queer reading’ to complicate concepts of celebrity culture

* *Class 10 Stars, Consumption, and Public Culture (2): Denise Ho, Kay Tse, and Charmaine Fong**

* Demonstrating celebrity consumption as a fundamental part of public culture
* Exploring how celebrities engage with fans in the public arena
* Assessing the star text and fandom of Denise Ho, Kay Tse, and Charmaine Fong in relation to the identity formation of Hong Kongers from 2010s to 2020s.

* *Class 11** **Stars in the Era of Platform Culture**

* Examining the availability of media platforms (e.g. Instagram, YouTube) and convergence media culture
* Evaluating changes in the celebrity culture alongside convergence culture
* Reflect on how convergence culture influences the formation of Hong Kong identity
* Case study: Serrin/ Leung Ka-yan (梁嘉茵) and Trial & Error (試當真)

* *Class 12 Discussion Panel (III)**

* Students will work in groups to create a presentation about their favourite Hong Kong micro-celebrity. Presentations should be submitted online via Blackboard.
* Each group will then be assigned to review another group’s presentation. They will analyze the assigned work and apply one concept from Class 9-11 in their critique.

* *Class 13 The Trans-Asian Influence of J-pop and K-pop Culture to Hong Kong**

* Evaluating the trans-Asian influence of J-pop and K-pop on Hong Kong celebrity culture in terms of industry, star images, and styles.
* Case study: Cookies and Mirror

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Lingnan: History and Society
courses.description:
Lingnan is located in the south of the Five Ridges, the mountain areas running from east to west that serve as a clear geographical and cultural demarcation between South and Central China. Lingnan plays a significant role in the historical development of Modern China. This course aims to overview 500 years of interweaving between Lingnan region, state and the world from the perspective of business, migration, knowledge and culture in the long-term history to understand Lingnan and enhance cultural recognition. At the same time, this course combines archival studies and fieldtrips. Besides discovering history through archive material, we will also visit museums, villages, temples, communities, and enterprises. Through contact with cultural and historical sites, students can deepen their understanding and perception of the social and cultural history of Lingnan.

Students from the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHKSZ) will jointly enroll in this course to promote cultural exchange and enhance mutual understanding. The course assessment methods will consist of individual assignments and group projects.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Not for History Majors.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000 or UGFN1000 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Develop a basic command of Lingnan history and deepen their understandings of Lingnan.
2. Acquire an understanding of the relations between Lingnan, China and the world and examine the openness and inclusiveness of Lingnan from historical perspectives.
3. Become familiar with some historical research methods and understand the opportunities and challenges in Greater Bay Area.

courses.course_syllabus:
1. Course in Shenzhen (3 days)

1. 1 【1st day morning】L01: 導論 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 嶺南的自然環境、歷史地理、人口民系等基本情況
* 歷史上中央王朝在嶺南地區的行政管理
* 明清嶺南的土地開發與宗族建構

議題：

* 嶺南在哪裡？
* 國家與嶺南的關係是什麼？
* 嶺南地區為何在明清時期進入快速發展時期？

1. 2 【1st day afternoon】L02: 世界貿易中的嶺南 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 朝貢貿易
* 16至18世紀的海上貿易
* 廣州制度（一口通商）

議題：

* 大航海時代之前嶺南與世界的貿易關係是怎樣的？
* 大航海時代對嶺南與世界的貿易網絡產生了什麼影響？

1. 3 【2nd day morning】L03: 全球化與嶺南移民 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 十九、二十世紀的嶺南移民：華商、華工與留學生
* 個案：深圳的海外移民、故事與記憶

議題：

* 深圳移民與嶺南、中國及世界的關係

1. 4 【2nd day afternoon】L04: 走向世界的「廣東文化」(lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 「廣東文化」的歷史建構過程
* 唐人街中的廣東元素
* 粵菜、粵劇的海外舞台

議題：

* 何謂「廣東文化」？
* 海外移民帶出去了哪些廣東文化？
* 如何認識廣東文化在海外的塑造與傳播？

1. 5 【3rd day morning】L05: 移民社會的包容與認同：改革開放的深圳經驗 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 深圳改革開放的人口變遷與移民政策
* 深圳城中村發展與城鄉身份轉型
* 深圳移民的個體經驗與口述歷史

議題：

* 誰是深圳人？
* 如何做一名深圳人？

1. 6 【3rd day afternoon】延伸討論：深圳田野考察 (4 hours)

主要內容：

* 理解小歷史與大歷史之間的關係
* 認識嶺南鄉村的族群、移民、經濟與文化等議題
* 認識深圳改革開放的歷史成就等

議題：

* 考察對象如何體現了嶺南地區與世界的聯繫？
* 如何從微觀史視角認識嶺南歷史？

田野考察 (三選一)

* 廣府文化類型考察（擬定）：南頭古城博物館+清平古墟+寶安古村落
* 客家文化類型考察（擬定）：深圳龍崗客家民俗博物館+坪山客家圍屋
* 改革開放重要史跡（擬定）：蛇口改革開放史跡遊徑

2. Course in Hong Kong (3 Days)

2. 1 【4th day morning】L06: 嶺南的開發與香港前期的發展 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 探討香港新界氏族遷徙與定居的故事
* 理解明清時期的香港與珠江三角洲的發展

議題：

* 香港的發展如何與嶺南的開發產生關係？

2. 2 【4th day afternoon】延伸討論：從建築看香港開埠的歷史 (field study: 4 hours)

主要內容：

* 香港開埠的歷史
* 理解早期殖民地政府的管治與華人移民社區的形成

2. 3 【5th day morning】L07: 連接中西的貿易橋樑：香港商業發展史 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 十九世紀香港如何取代廣州的貿易地位
* 什麼法律助長了香港的經濟地位？
* 香港的移民潮與社會經濟的發展

議題：

* 為什麼香港會由一個邊陲小島發展成為世界貿易中心？

2. 4 【5th day afternoon】L08: 傳統與認同：嶺南非物質文化遺產的創造 (lecture: 3 hours)

主要內容：

* 理解聯合國教科文組織所訂定的《保護非物質文化遺產公約》（2003年）
* 反思香港移民社會文化的多元性、包容性和傳承等問題

議題：

* 全球化脈絡中的國家與地方體系的文化是如何互動？

courses.title: Global Politics
courses.description:
(UGEC2352 is double-coded with GLSD2301.)

This course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to global politics, focusing in particular on its origins and historical evolution, its key concepts, major theoretical frameworks, main actors and institutions, the global architecture of power, and its dynamic nature in the process of globalization. It aims to offer students with the basic knowledge and analytical tools for making sense of current issues in global politics. It adopts a multi-disciplinary approach that integrates theoretical issues with regional case studies.

The course will first offer a general survey of the key concepts and major theoretical perspectives in the study of Global Politics (Liberalism, Realism, Social Constructivism and Marxist theory, etc.). It then proceeds to cover selected topics of global politics in the areas of War and Peace and the Clash of Civilization. It focuses on how world politics is transformed by globalization, with a particular focus on its impacts on issues concerning the identity and national pride, balance of power, peace and conflicts, borders and security, etc. Finally, the course will be concluded with the discussion of latest trends of global governance, with a particular focus on the emergency of international and regional organizations. Relevant real world examples and case studies will be adopted to illustrate the big ideas and key concepts of global politics.

This course intends to promote students’ appreciation of the role of ‘power’, ‘security’ and ‘justice’ in shaping the global political order nowadays. Students will gain deeper insights into not only latest developments in global political affairs, but also concepts and theories useful for further studies in politics, international relations, and global political economy. The course is designed to introduce essential concepts, major theoretical perspectives and basic mechanisms of global political order, allowing students to communicate issues in world politics effectively in group work and individually, in oral as well as written forms.

courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:

* 1.* *Describe the evolution of the global political order and identify how power relations is related to the peace and security of world politics;*

* 2.* *Understand and apply the basic concepts, theories and analytical approaches of global politics in understanding the interactions between states as well as the dynamics of the competition among great powers;*

* 3.* *Critically analyze the basic characteristics, process and institutions of global political order in* *national, regional and international* *levels;*

* 4.* *Describe and analyze the roles and functions of major international institutions and organizations, such as United Nations, in maintaining global peace and security;*

* 5.* *Analyze the role of the nation-states in the context of the globalized world*

* 6.* *Engage in debates on controversial world issues and reflect critically on different viewpoints**; and*

* 7.* *Develop better cross-cultural and geopolitical awareness necessary for a global citizen.*

If possible, seminar by invited guest will be arranged to provide students with insights into the debates and controversies in contemporary global political order.

* *Teaching Plan and Readings**

The following required readings only serve as the recommended references for this subject and you are encouraged to go to the library to explore other references on your own. Please feel free to consult the instructor as and when necessary. **Readings with asterisk\* are required references** that are most pertinent to part of the final quiz.

Notes:

1. This is a tentative keyword syllabus. We may adjust the pace and coverage based on your progress.

2. Always start with Heywood, and then read the rest as much as you can.

3. For full citations of the publications, please refer to § V above.

* *Part I: A Theoretical Framework in Understanding Global Politics**

* *Lecture 1: Introduction to Global Politics (I)**

Focus: Globalization, Global Politics and the Dynamics of Global Political Order

Key questions

- What do we mean by global politics?

- How does the idea of globalization challenge the inter-states politics?

Suggested readings:

- ***\*******Heywood****, ch.1*

- ***\*******Baylis****, ch.**1 and ch.2*

* *Lecture 2: Introduction to Global Politics (II)**

Focus: The Historical Background of Global Political Order; Globalization, States and Non-State Actors

Suggested readings:

- ***\*******Heywood****, ch.**2, ch.5 and ch.6*

Optional readings:

- *Jack Snyder, “One World, Rival Theories,” Foreign Policy, Nov/Dec 2004, pp.53-62.*

- *Stephen Krasner, “Think Again: Sovereignty,” Foreign Policy, Jan/Feb 2001, pp.20-29.*

- ***Karns****, M. P., Mingst, K. A., & Stiles, K. W. (2015). Nonstate actors: NGOs, Networks, and Social Movements. International organizations: The politics and processes of global governance (pp. 239-277). Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner.*

* *Lecture 3: Theories of Global Politics (I)**

Focus: Realism versus Liberalism

Key questions

- What makes realist perspectives so popular in the world? How does realism transform itself to fit the contemporary world? Key questions

- Is the global perpetual peace possible? If so, how can we attain global perpetual peace?

Suggested readings:

- ***\*******Heywood****, ch.3*

- ***\*******Baylis****, ch**6, ch.7 and ch.8*

Optional readings:

- ***R&R****, Kenneth Waltz, “The Anarchic Structure of World Politics”, pp.35-56.*

- ***R&R****, David Kang, “Hierarchy and Hegemony in International Politics”, pp.132-135*

- ***R&R****, Hans Morgenthau, “The Future of Diplomacy,” pp.136-145.*

- ***R&R****, Michael Doyle, “Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs”, pp.111-124.*

- ***Karns****, M. P., Mingst, K. A., & Stiles, K. W. (2015). The theoretical foundations* *of global governance. International organizations: The politics and* *processes of global governance (pp. 43-58). Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner.*

- *Waltz, Kenneth (1990). “Realist Thought and Neorealist Theory”. Journal of International Affairs. No. 44. Spring/Summer. pp. 21 – 37.*

- *Jervis, Robert (1978). “Cooperation under Security Dilemma”. World Politics. Vol. 30:2. pp. 167 – 214.*

- *Wang, Yuan Kang (2004). “Offensive Realism and the Rise of China”. Issues and Studies. Vol. 40:1. pp. 173 – 201.*

- *Doyle, Michael (1986). “Liberalism and World Politics”. American Political Science Review. Vol. 80:4. pp. 1151 – 1169.*

- *Richardson, James (1997). “Contending Liberalisms: Past and Present”. European Journal of International Relations. Vol. 3:1. pp. 5 – 33.*

- *Andrew Morvasick, “Taking Preference Seriously: A Liberal Theory of International Relations”, International Organization, vol.51, no.4, 1997, pp.513-553.*

* *Lecture 4: Theories of Global Politics (II)**

Focus: Social Constructivism and Marxist Theories

Key questions

- Is the world we lived really “real”? What is the role of identity in international relations? How do the norms and words shape the behaviours of the state?

- What is the relationship between capitalism and the global order? How hegemony is built and is there a way-out?

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Global Currents in Contemporary Art
courses.description:
(UGEC2371 is double-coded with FAAS2118.)
Contemporary art is diverse and expansive, and its timeline, topics, and aesthetic strategies, are continually redefined. This course offers an introduction into political and aesthetic issues addressed in global contemporary art, particularly since 1989 which marked the fall of the Iron Curtain and the first primordial “global” exhibition at Centre Pompidou. It will provide a variety of perspectives to discuss visions of the future presented by artists from diverse cultural backgrounds, who engage with such global issues as migration, borders, postcolonial conflicts, gender perspectives, environmental crisis, biodiversity, and digital capitalism. It will provide students with foundational knowledge on the emergence, developments, and challenges of global contemporary art discourses, as well as their contesting relationship with artistic autonomy and the society. We will examine a range of topics and methods employed by influential artists and thinkers in various geographies. This will provide a toolkit for understanding and curating contemporary art. To put critical thinking into practice, we will integrate exercises such as screenings and discussions, group projects, and exhibition proposals. Beyond art historical perspectives, we will also delve into questions regarding humans’ relationship with each other and the nonhumans, which are fundamental for understanding global currents and crisis addressed in contemporary art.

Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
After completing the course, students will be able to:

1. Identify major global art trends and key influential artworks from Europe, the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and Africa since 1989.
2. Examine the origins of and developments of the concept of global contemporary art in relation to postcolonial and posthuman discourses.
3. Recognize, differentiate, and explain the transcultural and transregional topics and issues that contemporary artists and curators engage in their works in the larger geopolitical contexts.
4. Build informed opinions on the quality and relevance of the arts since 1989, paying attention to their relations with global and local political and historical events.
5. Develop skills in speaking in public and organize research materials.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. **Introduction: Autonomy**

In this introduction session, we will cover some fundamental ideas and debates of global contemporary art, including the issues of autonomy, timeline, and social engagements, referencing theories and curatorial practices since 1989. Drawing from selected international museum collections, we will unpack a variety of institutional and geopolitical contexts that contributed to the formation of global contemporary art.

1. **Feminism**

This session will be devoted to feminist criticisms in art history, specifically the dialogues between women’s art and feminist movements between the 1970s and post 2000s. We will draw from several group exhibitions in Asia and the Americas post-1989 to discuss the issues of essentialism and representation in feminist Art histories.

1. **Queerness**

This session introduces various artistic approaches in deconstructing queer identities and bodies, mainly through selected case studies in digital and performance art. Students will be encouraged to compare these with discourses introduced during the last session, and discuss ways of decentering and expanding conventional feminist discourses.

1. **Migration**

In this session, we will examine the concepts of mapping and displacements in the context of specific political and environmental crises. To do so, selections of contemporary gallery films by minority or immigrant artists will be screened, followed by a discussion.

1. **Transculturality and Border Art**

Drawing from transcultural studies and border studies, we will examine several media and performance art works as well as curatorial approaches that cope with cultural conflicts and hybridity. Selected case studies include *Magiciens de la terre* in Paris in 1989, the Whitney Biennale in New York, Asian Biennale in Taichung, and documenta Kassel.

1. **Colonialism**

This session focuses on visual art creations that address natural resource extraction and indigenous rights issues. It will start with an introduction to primitivism in modern art, then move on to reactions to Imperialism in works by South-East Asian and African artists as new nation states and identities emerge.

1. **Indigenous Art and Postcolonialism**

We will talk about First Nations land justice and reconciliation in this session. An institutional history of indigenous art will be covered first, then selected contemporary practices and their cultural representations under specific government policies. Particular attention will be given to discourses in Canada, Australia, and the New Zealand.

1. **Environmentalism**

This session introduces discourses of eco-art and the Anthropocene. We will also draw from political ecology to discuss artistic approaches to environmental justice. Issues of community engagement and green washing will be attended.

1. **Bio Art**

This session provides an overview on the history of bio art, its application in industries, the public reception, and the ethical issues.

1. **Digital Capitalism**

In this session, we will look at artistic reflections on surveillance and digital capitalism through concrete examples. We will screen selected essay films that engages with data discrimination, surveillance infrastructure, and deepfake, followed by a discussion.

1. **Asian Diaspora**

In this session, we will discuss the definitions of diaspora and the Sinophone through visual arts. We will look at artists outside of Mainland China who engage with “Chinese” identities differently. Works by such artists as Ian Cheng, Patty Chang, Musquiqui Chihying, and Lee Wen will be discussed.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Visual and Material Culture of the Ming Dynasty
courses.description:
(UGEC2391 is double-coded with FAAS2106.)
This course discusses the changes of visual and material cultures of the Ming dynasty through studying objects, images and texts. Topics including ceramics, lacquerwares, gold and precious stones, textiles, prints and other art and artefacts made for people from all walks of life will be covered. Through introducing representative images and objects and different trends of social development of the Ming period, such as religious fervor, sumptuous consumption, and erotic culture, the course aims at exploring how the emergence of classic images and artefacts are linked to the political, economic, religious, technological and aesthetic development of a time.

courses.course_syllabus:
The following topics will be covered in the course:

(1) Visual Culture & Material Culture

Introduction to the concepts of visual culture and material culture and their application to the study of art and culture of the Ming dynasty in the past decades.

(2) Ming Society and Ming Cities

Discussing the social and geographical structure of the Ming empire, especially the relationship between the emperor and his court in the capital (Nanjing and Beijing), Ming princes in their princedoms, officials, businessmen and literati in Jiangnan and other major provinces.

(3) Material I: Ceramics and Everyday Utensils

Technological advancements in ceramic production in the imperial porcelain factory at Jingdezhen, Jiangxi and the consumption of different types of ceramics in Ming society.

(4) Material II: Gold, Precious Stones and Body Accessories

The import of precious stones in the Ming dynasty and the discovery of personal accessories made of gold and precious stones from tombs in conformity to/ in violation of sumptuous laws.

(5) Material III: Textiles and Costumes

Technological advancements in dyeing and weaving and the clothing fashion in late Ming Jiangnan.

(6) Material IV: Lacquers and Ornaments

The cultural and technological exchange in lacquer production between China, Japan and Ryukyu, and the increasing emphasis on creating visual effect in object production.

(7) Material V: Prints and Books Culture

Technological advancements in printing in the late Ming period and the spread of visual knowledge across different social strata through catalogues of material objects (such as patterned papers and ink cakes) and illustrated books.

(8) Case Studies: Representative Images across Different Media

The use of the same images (such as *qin-qi-shu-hua*, i.e. playing *qin-*zither, chess, reading and appreciating paintings) in different material objects and their changing meaning through the Ming dynasty.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Popular Culture in Contemporary China
courses.description:
(UGEC2434 is double-coded with CHES2103.)

This rise of China as a global power has drawn critical attention from all over the world from various perspectives. This course will approach this phenomenon from the angle of popular culture. Examining contemporary Chinese popular culture in the Chinese Mainland, Hong Kong, and Taiwan, this course considers the process of globalization, cultural exchanges among China, Europe, America, and Africa, the cultural flows among East Asian popular culture, particularly, with Japan and Korea, as well as interactions among Sinophone communities around the world. This course takes an interdisciplinary methodology, incorporating materials in the form of literature, films, TV series, pop music, reality shows, online forums, video games, and so on, to explore how economic development, technological innovations, and political atmosphere shape the youth culture, gender dynamics, class structure and many other issues on a daily basis.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Popular Religions in Hong Kong
courses.description: This course studies the "little" religious traditions in Hong Kong in the context of South China. The so-called "little" traditions are different from the three "great" Chinese traditions: Taoism, Buddhism and Confucianism. The "little" traditions are often known as popular religions or common religions. They represent the religious orientation of the majority of Chinese people. By expanding our horizon from globalized, highly abstract and univocal systems of thought to domestic localized oral and non-elite mentalities, we are striving to represent more accurately the heterogeneity of religious experience of Hong Kong people. Through the study of popular religions in Hong Kong, this course hopes to enrich students with a better understanding of both the structure and the dynamics of Hong Kong society as well as its local culture.

courses.learning_outcomes:
香港民間宗教，同學日常生活或已有聽聞，但之前未有學術探討與實地考察去瞭解，本科提供了此學習內容和途徑。同學通過大課、小組導修及兩次考察，基本上吸收和掌握科目要點，即香港民間宗教與傳統社會文人之間關係。

課堂上講及的民間宗教活動，如「太平清醮與地域社會」，同學對其源流、地方神祇和族群都加了認識。特別是實地考察，同學意見反映是頗能與課堂教學配合，引起他們對有關課題的興趣和深究。

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Chinese Temples and Festivals
courses.description:
(UGEC2500 is double-coded with CURE2375.)

This course is a study of Chinese temples and festivals. Temples are cultural heritages which preserve as mute testimony to local history. Their structures and the use of ornaments also reflect traditional architectural characteristics. "Jie dan" (festivals), including birthdays of the gods and jiao rituals, are the ritual activities being held for prosperity in folk culture. The belief system, indigenous custom, human diasporas as well as community cohesiveness of the Chinese can be illustrated from both temples and festivals in China and Hong Kong.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Big Issues of Globalization
courses.description: In this course we will review the major issues surrounding the process of globalization in the contemporary world. We will get behind these issues and discuss the backgrounds, manifestations, and implications of these issues on global development. Issues including the economic globalization, the global financial system and crisis, political governance and globalization, social impacts of globalization, the globalization of culture, the environment and globalization and anti-globalization movement will be covered, but additional issues and special topics may be added when necessary. The social scientific theories of globalization will serve as a background for our discussions but we are also going to emphasize the relevance of globalization to our everyday life.

Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1)To recognize the key concepts, theories, salient patterns and impacts of the major issues of contemporary globalization.

(2)To interpret and discuss the relevance to and impacts of globalization on everyday life experiences and current affairs.

(3)To apply concepts and issues covered in this course to new phenomenon related to contemporary globalization.

(4)To understand and evaluate the various normative positions over the major issues of contemporary globalization.

(5)To demonstrate the mastery of skills in information collection, retrieval and analysis, as well as the use of such information in the analysis of concrete situations of everyday life experience.
courses.course_syllabus:
Big Issues of Globalization

1. Introduction: Globalization as Everyday Life
2. Approaches to Globalization
3. History of Globalization
4. Investment, Trade and Global Division of Labor
5. Globalization and Migration
6. Cultural Globalization
7. End of State?
8. Clash of Civilization?
9. Globalization and Environment
10. Globalization and Inequality
11. Anti-Globalization Movement and Other Responses
12. Conclusion: Winners, Losers, You and Me.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: News Analysis
courses.description:
(UGEC2621 is double-coded with COMM2910.)

Theories and methods in news sociology in understanding the news-making process and its impacts on the product itself and the society. Students also learn to conduct their own analysis of news in local or foreign media.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2621 is double-coded with COMM2910. 
Not for GCOM; COMM Majors; and students who have taken COMM2210, 2910 or UGEC2623. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.learning_outcomes:
The aim of this course is three-fold. First, it is designed to introduce students to various conceptual approaches to news. Second, the "media logic" of each news medium will be analysed. Third, students shall zero in on some key aspects of news and use conceptual tools to analyse various news phenomena. Emphasis will be on the local news media.

This course is intended to sharpen students' conceptual framework and generic attribute of analytical thinking.
courses.course_syllabus: This course deals with some conceptual issues such as the nature and significance of news, frameworks of news analysis, models of news production, market-driven journalism, and the social roles of news. It will also focus on the "grammar" of each news medium, including newspaper, radio, television, and news website. The news format, layout, strengths and weaknesses of each medium will be examined. In addition, various factors affecting news agendas, news sources and news angles, news benefactors and victims, international news reporting, as well as some news trends in recent years will be studied.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Internet, Digital Media and Information Society
courses.description:
(UGEC2624 is double-coded with COMM2940.)

This course aims to examine a number of key issues that are closely related to developments in Internet and digital media. The advent of communication technologies has brought tremendous changes to media environments. Media convergence and participatory culture are two most notable emerging trends that have contributed to new forms of media production and consumption. Students will be introduced to key concepts and perspectives in appreciating, analyzing and evaluating such trends. Through case studies about social media, streaming entertainment, Internet celebrities, networked social movements and digital surveillance culture, etc, students will review the many tacit assumptions about Internet in their everyday life.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2624 is double-coded with COMM2940.Not for Journalism and Communication; Global Communication Majors; and students who have taken COMM2940. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1 Phenomena, problems and issues**

In this introductory class, we will examine a few recent viral cases in social media and discuss two recurring themes, namely convergence and participation, in this course.

* *Week 2 When old media were new…**

In this class, we will dive into a few key episodes in the history of communication technologies. We will review and discuss how various factors have contributed to the invention and development of communication fads.

* *Week 3 Mediated memories: How we remember and are remembered?**

Communication technologies have been important memory devices in human history. We will trace how communication technologies co-evolved with memory practices.

* *Week 4 Social media: How we connect and are connected?**

What media are not “social media”? Media always facilitate networking in different forms. We will reconsider what differentiates the social media we know of today from previous generations of social media.

* *Week 5 Dating apps and romance**

The meanings of ‘romance’ and ‘intimacy’ have undergone sweeping changes with the advent of dating apps in smartphones. In this class, we will examine the features of these apps and uncover their assumptions underlying ‘love’.

* *Week 6 MOOC and learning**

Massive Open Online Courses are introducing new forms of teaching, learning and academic accreditation. In a broader sense, how has Internet transformed learning? We will critically evaluate some popular claims in this aspect.

* *Week 7 KOL and public opinions**

Key Opinion Leaders are also known as social influencers or sometimes internet celebrities. They are seen to exert increasing influence in ‘public opinions’ or ‘public sentiments’.　In this class, we will revisit earlier communication theory regarding two-step flow of information and see how Internet has brought new practices in shaping public opinions.

* *Week 8 Streaming media and entertainment**

In this class, we will focus on the case of streaming media and discuss how entertainment is changed in the Internet era. We will also consider how this in turn affects the production, distribution and consumption of media products.

* *Week 9 - 10 Haters and comment culture**

Comment culture is a notable Internet phenomenon. Instead of looking at ‘likes’, we focus on the mechanisms behind ‘dislikes’ and the behaviors of ‘haters’.

* *Week 11 Protest mobilization and social movements**

Internet is seen to be a key factor in protest mobilization. We will examine some key elements in social movements and discuss how social media, for example, have contributed (or not) in the mobilization process.

* *Week 12 Surveillance and sensor society**

The classic ‘big brother’ thesis is discussed with a careful consideration of many emerging practices in surveillance and self-surveillance. The idea of ‘sensor society’ will be introduced to see how we are (in)voluntarily contributing to a productive surveillance culture.

* *Week 13 Hello future!**

In this final class, we will reconsider the two central themes of convergence and participation and make both informed and wild guesses for the future.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Media and Social Development in Mainland China
courses.description:
(UGEC2634 is double-coded with COMM2140.)

The course is designed around two major themes, namely media and social development in Mainland China since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. Using key concepts and theories from the political economy of media and developmental communication studies, it introduces students to different periods of media reform and social change from the era of Chairman Mao to the period of "harmonious society". Emphasis is attached to post-1989 media regulatory systems, media industrialization, and their influence on the meeting of such developmental goals as poverty alleviation, democratization, and communication empowerment.

The course will examine Mainland China's key media sectors including the printing press (newspapers and magazines), film and broadcasting media (radio and TV), and new networked communication tools (Internet and mobile phone) as well as alternative social formations through Internet activism, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and transnational developmental projects. The course will identify and discuss several ongoing debates, and the ensuing actions, held by different stakeholders, including governmental officials, media producers, educators, activists, international agencies, and the general audiences. Wider implications to public policy will be identified. There will also be discussions of current affairs related to media and social development in the country.

Students will be able to describe the key characteristics of contemporary Mainland Chinese media and their roles in facilitating or obstructing development towards the ideals of a "new China".

courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be able to describe key characteristics of media in Mainland China.

2. Students will be able to discuss how media influences social development and how new social formations trigger media reform in Mainland China.

3. Students will be able to identify phases of media and social development in Mainland China and differentiate policymaking rationales in different media sectors (printing, broadcasting, networked media) and types of social movements.

4. Students will be able to discuss competing arguments about the role of media reform in China's modernization drive.

5. Students will be able to produce a media text that offers a critique to one of the historical periods, media industries, or controversial issues covered in the course.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course consists of five main parts: (I) theories of media, communication and social development (week 1 and 2); (II) history of media transformation in Mainland China since 1949 (week 3 and 4); (III) key media sectors (week 5 to 7); (IV) social movements and campaigns (week 8 to 10); and (V) institutional stakeholders (week 11 and 12). In each part, there will be a mixture of conceptual and practical information, of consensus and controversies, and of historical knowledge and current affairs. The class will also look at different disadvantaged social groups and their relationship with various media sectors and stakeholders both within and outside officialdom.

The following is an outline of the course:

* *Week 1 Introduction: Ideals of "New China"**

The first class will introduce students to (a) the pursuit of a "New China" that gave legitimacy to the rise of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) since the May Fourth Movement, and (b) classical theories of media and national development between 1950s and 1980s. It will also discuss the concept of 'social development' and give an overview of the course's core content.

* Key concepts: "New China", nation building, communication and development*

* *Week 2 Communist Media Theories: Political Control and Social Development**

This class discusses Leninist press theory, its evolution in the Chinese party-state, and the rationale behind this historical transformation, including politico-economic considerations as well as trends in cultural and technological change. Key ideas of the mass line and ICTD (information and communication technologies and development) will also be discussed in the case of rural development.

* Key concepts: Leninist press theory, party-state, political control, the mass line, ICTD, rural development*

* *Week 3 and 4 Past and Present**

These two classes differentiate media and social development in Mainland China into three historical periods: 1949-1978; 1978-1989; and 1989-date. What defines these periods? How are they different? Did previous periods pave the way for later trends of marketization and partial liberalization in the post-1989 era?

* Key concepts: The Maoist era, pre-1989 media reform, post-1989 reform, marketization, partial liberalization*

* *Weeks 5 to 7 Key Media Sectors**

Zooming into China's printing media (newspaper and magazines), film and broadcasting media (radio and TV), and new networked media (Internet and mobile phone), these three classes provide a sector-specific analysis of China's media systems and their contributions to meeting goals of social development. Issues of censorship and regulation will be introduced. Debates on the digital divide will also be discussed.

* Key concepts: printing media, film, broadcasting media, networked media, censorship, regulation, digital divide*

* *Weeks 8 to 10 Social Movements and Campaigns**

These three classes focus on official efforts to modernize China using traditional and new media channels as well as alternative communication empowerment projects such as those led by domestic labor NGOs, environmental groups, and transnational civil society players. Studies in minority-nationality regions and with regard to disadvantaged groups such as women will be discussed along with the official project of "constructing new socialist countryside".

* Key concepts: "constructing new socialist countryside", activism, empowerment, feminist activism, environmental movement, minority nationalities, transnational civil society*

* *Week 11 and 12 Institutional Stakeholders**

We will first return to China's media regulatory frameworks centered on the CCP's Central Propaganda Division (CPD) as well as several ministry-level governing bodies whose bureaucratic systems extend to lower levels of the party-state. Then in Week 12, we will look into China's journalism education system as another key institutional stakeholder. To what extent are the regulators and educators facilitating or hindering overall social development? Why? How could they do better? How could college students in Hong Kong play a meaningful role interacting with the stakeholders?

* Key concepts: CPD, local state, media governance, journalism education, democratization*

* *Week 13 Student Group Presentations and Course Wrap-Up**

Students will present their final projects in the last class, which will end with the instructor's wrap-up of the course.

courses.description:
(UGEC2653 is double-coded with ANTH2310.)

This course looks at the relationship between gender and culture, by comparing women and men in societies with different modes of production and social organization. Through analysing gender roles, enculturation process, kinship, division of labour by gender, power and control and social development, students will understand how culture influences the concept of gender and its related behaviour among human groups.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Ethnographies of Japan
courses.description:
(UGEC2657 is double-coded with ANTH2327.)
This course provides an introduction to contemporary Japanese society and culture. In the popular imagination, Japan occupies a complex and often contradictory position. It is home to futuristic anime and an aging population, picturesque villages and dolphin hunts, high-end cameras and the widespread use of quaint fax machines. Engaging with anthropological literature, students will learn to analyze, discuss, and write about various issues and cultural features of Japan, including youth, popular culture, self, family, labor, medicine, and health. An overarching theme will be how Japanese culture and society is changing in the transition to a highly aged society. We will examine persistent cultural patterns as well as the emergence of new forms of social life as residents of Japan grapple with smaller families, precarity, migration, and a rising population of older people. Students will learn how to apply theoretical concepts from anthropology and think critically about Japanese culture and its portrayals in the media. The ethnographic approaches and theoretical perspectives covered in this class will be applicable to other cultural contexts. Since Hong Kong, China, and Korea are following Japan’s path of population aging, this course provides an opportunity to explore cultural issues that have a local and regional significance.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
UGEC2657 is double-coded with ANTH2327.
Not for Anthropology Majors; and students who have taken ANTH2327.
Co-requisite: Any course with "UGFH" or "UGFN" as prefix
courses.learning_outcomes:
* Students will acquire a robust knowledge of contemporary Japanese society and culture. They will develop an understanding of cultural diversity within Japan and the broad shifts associated with population aging.

* Students will gain the ability to apply anthropological theory to analyze Japanese society and culture. In conjunction, students will learn to critically evaluate scholarly and media portrayals of Japan. These critical faculties will also be relevant for understanding their own or other societies in daily life as well as for future anthropological studies.

* Students will develop their writing skills. In addition to conventional academic essays, students will learn to write ethnographically about a specific site. Through writing, students will gain skills in communication of their own observations and perspectives on cultural features. These skills can be used for further academic study as well as personal and professional life.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part I: Foundations of Japanese Culture and Society

Week 1. What is Japanese culture?

* This lesson introduces the concept of culture and gives a brief history on the sociocultural and geographical boundaries of Japan.

Week 2. Foundational Works

* This lesson provides students with an introduction to early major writings about Japan, including early European and American visitors to Japan.

Week 3. Myths of Japaneseness

* This session will examine of common media tropes about Japan and the pseudo-scholarly genre of writing known as *Nihonnjinron*. It explores forms of ethnocentricism, conceptions of cultural uniqueness, and nationalism in post WWII Japan.

Week 4. Traditions and Inventions

* This session focuses on the ways that traditions created and how people use them to give meaning to life. Through a discussion of *bushido*, the class will illuminate the recent invention of traditions popularly considered ancient and timeless in Japan.

Week 5. Health and the Body

* The session provides a conceptual overview of how people in Japan understand their bodies, health, and illness. Particular attention will be paid to longevity and issues involved in aging.

Week 6. Gift-giving and Ritual

* An exploration of situational, lifecycle, and calendar-based gift-giving and ritual in contemporary Japan.

II. The Life Cycle in an Aging Japan

Week 7. Love, Marriage, and Children

* This session provides an overview of romantic relationships, including non-heteronormative relationships, and reasons for low fertility in Japan. Romance in late life will also be part of the discussion.

Week 8. Childhood and Schooling

* Focusing on preschool through high school, this session examines the ways children are taught to become adults in Japanese society.

Week 9. Cute and *Otaku*

* This class explores the origins of subcultures in Japan and how they are co-opted by the state and companies. It will highlight the ways that young people’s participation in these subcultures receives blame for low fertility.

Week 10. Labor, Precarity, and Class

* This session is an examination of the changes in Japanese labor following WWII in relation to security, gender, and socioeconomic class. It will highlight how precarious working conditions lead individuals to delay or avoid marriage and having children.

Week 11. Gender

* Students will learn about how gender intersects with family, work, and social roles. This session will highlight conventional roles of the male “salaryman” and the housewife, paying attention to female caregiving for older family members.

Week 12. Aging and the End of Life

* This session examines the experiences of late life ideals for death .

Week 13. Atomic Radiation and the Plight of Older People after Fukushima

* A broad discussion of Japan complicated relationship with radioactive decay, including atomics bombs, Godzilla, and the meltdown in Fukushima. Particular attention will be paid to case of aging survivors of the atomic bombs and older people’s communities displaced after the disasters following the earthquake on 11.3.2011.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Culture and Business
courses.description:
(UGEC2662 is double-coded with ANTH2510.)

Culture is ubiquitous in every aspect of societies, including how we do business. This course will examine the role of culture in contemporary business and study work and management in industrial societies anthropologically. Students will be introduced to the cultural logics of business practices, particularly business operations, organization and management through ethnographic explorations of different cultures, locales and sociohistorical settings. The aims of the course are twofold. First, it reveals cultural aspects and the cultural mechanisms of business. It shows the significance of culture in the business world, as well as the cultural significance of business. Second, it attempts to put anthropology into business practice. It demonstrates to students how anthropological knowledge and methodologies can be applied to business operations and help to achieve business goals. By examining the themes including but not limited to the indoctrination of work ethics, labor relations, gender and racial issues in the workplace, capitalism and its discontents, and responses to and actions upon market capitalism in terms of both production and consumption, the course attends to these Sustainable Development Goals: No Poverty (SDG#1), Gender Equality (SDG#5), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG#8), Reduced Inequalities (SDG#10), Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG#12), and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG#17).

courses.course_syllabus:
The course is structured in three parts. *Part I Culture in Business* explores the cultural dimensions of workplaces and corporate management. We begin with an overview of the temporal and spatial reconfigurations since industrialization in order to discern modern work ethics, followed by explorations of dynamics in the workplace. Next, we will explore discourses in shaping corporate operations and management, and consider (and challenge) the ideas of economization, maximization, auditing and accountability. This part decodes life in business settings, and practices in corporations. *Part II Business Ventures in the Globalizing World* situates the discussions in current trends of capitalism. We will look into what makes us buy and spend, and how traditional values and modern business practices mingle. It raises the question of whether we are really emancipated under the fashion of decentralization by exploring the gig economy and the phenomenon of self-enterprising. We will also examine how we can build a more inclusive, diverse and equal society by finding a new way out from the existing business ideologies and practices. *Part III Anthropology and the Business World* discusses how to apply anthropology in business settings, looking into how and why anthropology and anthropologists are important to the private sector, and broadly speaking, to the modern capitalist world. The course concludes by contemplating whether business is really business.

Overall, through the examinations of how we are taught to work, produce, and buy, the imperative of gender and racial stereotypes in the workplace, turns in capitalism and the rise of new economies and the pertinent social and cultural phenomena, the course addresses the following Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): No Poverty (SDG#1), Gender Equality (SDG#5), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG#8), Reduced Inequalities (SDG#10), Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG#12), and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG#17).

* *Core topics:**

Week 1 Course Introduction

Week 2 Seeing Business Anthropologically **(SDGs 17)**

* *Part I Culture in Business**

Week 3 Space, Time and Work Ethics **(SDGs 8, 10)**

Week 4 Gender, Race/Ethnicity, and Communication in the Workplace **(SDGs 5, 8, 10)**

Week 5 Corporatization, Economization and Maximization **(SDGs 1, 8, 10, 12)**

Week 6 Audit Culture and Accountability **(SDGs 8)**

Week 7 Mid-term Test

* *Part II Business Ventures in the Globalizing World**

Week 8 The Making of Consumers **(SDGs 10, 12)**

Week 9 Fieldtrip to a Social Enterprise/ a Social Innovation Project/ an exhibition about reindustrialization in Hong Kong

Week 10 The Gig Economy and Self-enterprising **(SDGs 1, 8, 10)**

Week 11 Ethical-Political Consumerism and Social Entrepreneurialism **(SDGs 1, 5, 8, 10, 12, 17)**

* *Part III Anthropology and the Business World**

Week 12 Applying Anthropology to Business Practice **(SDGs 10, 17)**

Week 13 Conclusion: Is Business Really Business?

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Sports and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2664 is double-coded with ANTH2390.)

This course will examine the role and importance of sports in different societies and cultures, in the present and the past. Sports are often thought of as trivial, or as unimportant games to amuse young people. But in the wealthiest countries, sports represent huge portions of GDP and are important topics of daily conversation. Almost half the world watched the 2010 football/soccer World Cup. Sports have been compared to religions in their ability to unite people and to inspire fanatical devotion.

The academic study of sports is interdisciplinary, with contributions from psychologists, historians, gender studies scholars, sociologists and anthropologists. This course will take an interdisciplinary approach while emphasizing anthropology’s focus on culture, on the experience of participants, and on both symbolic and political-economy aspects of sports. Topics will include Race and Performance, Sports and Rituals, Sports as Moral Education, Gender and Sexuality in Sport, Sports and Nationalism, Globalization of Sport, the Olympics, and Sports Stars and the Media. Students will be expected to do a research project for the course.

courses.subject: UGEC
courses.title: Social Media and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2665 is double-coded with ANTH2540.)

This course addresses the ways in which social media and other related interactions in cyberspace have become a central element in the everyday lives of humans across the globe in the 21st Century. Our modern lives are now largely interwoven with digital technologies that have not only changed our own cultures, but also have brought forth new cultural forms through mobile phone technologies, networked “smart”-products, and cultural groupings only possible through digital means. The course approaches the anthropology of these digital cultures through its main themes—the transformation and expansion of social media, social research online, the intermixing of our online and offline lives, critical social issues of online lives, and the question of posthumanism. These themes are addressed explicitly in the course, and are also the subtexts of the different lectures, readings, and project work. Students will learn the techniques of online fieldwork and referencing. They will explore a diverse array of new ethnographies on social media: on gender, political movements, online dating, hacking, and gaming culture. These ethnographies also serve to model online social research and provide examples of methodology and design. The social consequences of cyberspace are addressed in the topics of internet pornography, addiction, surveillance, activism, and social networking. Gender and identity issues are a continuous theme throughout the course, highlighting how online lives accentuate already existing dynamics. Hong Kong connections to these subjects will also be critically discussed, often drawing on topical themes presented on blogs and forums. Students will learn of the philosophical questions of posthumanism and the nature of technologically mediated human culture. This serves as a philosophical ballast to the course allowing students to reflect personally on their own experiences and how technology has and will continue to shape their lives. The role of anthropology in understanding and capturing human culture in this context anchors on the investigation of how technology is possibly making us ‘more’ human than previous forms of cultural life.
